Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Energy Corporation Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to John Smith, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

John Smith: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Energy Corporation's Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Jenkins, Chief Financial Officer; David Rodriguez, Chief Operating Officer; Steve Harlan, VP of Exploration; Lisa Chen, VP of Marketing; Emma Patel, Chief Sustainability Officer; and Raj Singh, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we make today may be forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

I will now turn the call over to Mike Thompson.

Mike Thompson: Thank you, John Smith, and good morning, everyone. Apex Energy Corporation delivered solid results in Q3 2024, driven by strong operational performance and favorable commodity prices. We achieved robust midstream segment performance with record transportation volumes and ongoing infrastructure development. I'm particularly pleased with our EBITDA growth, up significantly year-over-year due to pricing tailwinds and volume gains. We are focused on lifting costs per BOE, where we've driven meaningful reductions through targeted initiatives. Further, we are prioritizing capital allocation across dividends, share buybacks, and high-return reinvestments. We continue to adjust operating expenses per BOE downward with disciplined cost management. We are advancing refining segment performance through higher throughput, resilient margins, and efficiency gains. We are evaluating capital expenditure breakdowns across drilling, completion, and facilities, coming in under budget. Finally, we are taking steps to expand exploration and drilling activities with strong well results and clear future plans.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, Mike. As Mike mentioned, we had a strong quarter. Our revenue was $5.2 billion, up 20% year-over-year. Operating income was $1.1 billion, and net income was $850 million. We generated $1.2 billion in free cash flow and returned $800 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Our balance sheet remains strong, with $4.5 billion in debt and $2.1 billion in cash.

Good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to dive into our Midstream segment performance for the quarter, with a particular focus on transportation volumes and infrastructure development. As you know, Midstream remains a cornerstone of our integrated model, generating stable, fee-based cash flows through our 12,000 miles of pipelines, 50 million barrels of crude storage, and extensive natural gas processing and fractionation assets across key U.S. basins. In Q3, the segment delivered another quarter of robust results, posting revenues of $1.2 billion, up 15% year-over-year, and adjusted EBITDA of $850 million, a 18% increase, with margins expanding to 71% from 68% last year. This resilience underscores our strategy of long-term, take-or-pay contracts—now 92% of our midstream revenues—insulating us from commodity volatility amid WTI averaging $78 per barrel and Henry Hub gas at $2.85 per MMBtu.

Let me start with transportation volumes, which were the standout driver this quarter. Total throughput across our system hit a record 4.8 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, or MBOE/d, up 12% sequentially from Q2 and 22% year-over-year. Breaking it down by commodity: Crude oil volumes averaged 2.2 million barrels per day, or MMbbl/d, a 25% Y/Y surge, primarily fueled by Permian Basin outperformance. Our Longhorn Pipeline, which we expanded to 850,000 bbl/d capacity last year in JV with DCP Midstream, ran at 98% utilization, transporting record Permian WTI to the Gulf Coast. This was complemented by our wholly-owned Eagle Ford Express system, averaging 650,000 bbl/d at full utilization, benefiting from associated gas production growth as operators like EOG Resources ramped up D&C activity amid $60-plus NYMEX strip prices.

Natural gas transportation clocked in at 5.2 billion cubic feet per day, or Bcf/d—a 10% Y/Y increase—led by our Haynesville and Marcellus assets. The Haynesville Highway Pipeline, our 2.5 Bcf/d artery connecting to the CGT Haynesville pipeline grid, achieved 95% utilization, capturing incremental volumes from Chesapeake Energy's aggressive drilling program. In Appalachia, our MARC-1 line to TGP interconnects moved 1.8 Bcf/d, up 8% Y/Y, as dry gas production responds to LNG export demand from Gulf Coast facilities like Plaquemines LNG, now online and pulling 1.3 Bcf/d from our system.

NGL volumes were equally strong at 425,000 bbl/d, up 16% Y/Y, driven by fractionation ramps at our Mont Belvieu complex. Here, we processed 420,000 bbl/d through our five fractionation trains, with ethane rejection dynamics flipping positive—reject rates fell to 15% from 35% last year—as ethane cracks widened to $0.15/gal on Mont Belvieu, incentivizing producers like ExxonMobil to keep rich gas flowing.

These volume gains weren't accidental; they reflect basin-level trends. Permian crude production hit 6.2 MMbbl/d per EIA data, overwhelming local takeaway and pushing basis differentials to -$2.50/bbl at Waha Hub before narrowing to -$0.50 on our expansions. Similarly, Haynesville gas output climbed 12% Y/Y to 15 Bcf/d, pressuring Agua Dulce pricing until our infrastructure absorbed the surge. Regional commentary: Texas Gulf Coast remains our growth engine, with 60% of volumes destined for export terminals like our JV Corpus Christi Crude Terminal, loading 1.1 MMbbl/d for destinations including India and Europe. Appalachia provides defensive stability with 85% contracted volumes to power plants and LNG, while the Bakken contributed steadily at 250,000 bbl/d via our Dakota Pride Pipeline.

Shifting to infrastructure development, we're executing a disciplined $2.8 billion capex program for 2024, with 65% already deployed YTD, targeting 8-10% annual EBITDA growth through 2026. Key highlights: Permian expansions: We mechanically completed the Apex Permian Connector, a 42-inch, 550 MMcf/d lateral tying Waha producers directly to our Longhorn system. This $450 million greenfield project, backed by 20-year take-or-pay from Occidental and Pioneer, entered partial service in late September at 400 MMcf/d, with full ramp to 550 MMcf/d by Q1 2025. It's already capturing 20 MMcf/d from new Diamondback pads.

NGL infrastructure: At Mont Belvieu, our Train 6 fractionation unit—450,000 bbl/d nameplate—hit 95% mechanical completion ahead of its Q4 in-service. This $650 million investment, financed 50/50 with Enterprise Products Partners, addresses fractionation deficits projected by RBN Energy at 150,000 bbl/d through 2025. We've locked in 85% of capacity with fee-based contracts from ConocoPhillips and MPLX.

Gulf Coast LNG takeaway: Responding to the Biden Administration's LNG pause, we're advancing the $300 million Apex LNG Link, a 1.2 Bcf/d pipeline from Haynesville headers to Golden Pass LNG. FERC approval secured in July; construction starts Q1 2025, with FID from QatarEnergy underpinning 70% utilization.

Tech initiatives: We're deploying AI-driven leak detection and predictive maintenance across 70% of our crude lines, partnering with Baker Hughes on fiber-optic DAS systems. This has reduced downtime 25% Y/Y and positions us for ESG compliance under PHMSA's mega-rule, targeting zero unreported incidents.

Strategically, these investments yield 12-15% unlevered IRRs at current volumes, with 90% of capex generating DCF within 5 years. We've hedged 80% of 2025 transportation tariffs via our LIBOR-plus structure, locking in $0.85/bbl on crude and $0.12/Dth on gas. Looking ahead, we guide Q4 midstream EBITDA at $875-900 million, implying full-year growth of 20%. Long-term, we're prioritizing Permian-to-Gulf flows amid 500,000 bbl/d of new takeaway coming online industry-wide, while exploring carbon capture tie-ins—like our MOUs with Occidental for DAC on Permian CO2 streams—to future-proof assets.

We're well-positioned to capture the next leg of U.S. hydrocarbon exports, with LNG capacity doubling to 20 Bcf/d by 2027 per Poten & Partners.

I'll now dive right into our Adjusted EBITDA performance, which was a standout this quarter and underscores the strength of our portfolio amid a resilient macro environment. For the quarter, Adjusted EBITDA reached $1.65 billion, representing a robust 24% year-over-year increase from $1.33 billion in Q3 2023. On a trailing twelve-month basis, this brings our full-year run-rate Adjusted EBITDA to $6.2 billion, up 22% from the prior year's $5.1 billion. This outperformance exceeded our guidance midpoint by 8% and reflects a combination of favorable pricing dynamics, disciplined volume growth, and aggressive cost-out initiatives across our key basins.

First, realized pricing provided a significant tailwind. Our blended realized price per barrel of oil equivalent—or boe—averaged $78.50/boe this quarter, up 15% from $68.20/boe in Q3 2023. This was driven by stronger Brent crude benchmarks, which averaged $86/bbl versus $78/bbl last year, supported by sustained OPEC+ production cuts and robust global demand, particularly from Asia amid LNG export growth. In the U.S., our WTI realizations hit $81.20/bbl, benefiting from a narrow WTI-Brent spread of just $4.50/bbl—our tightest in three years—thanks to improved Gulf Coast infrastructure like the new Matterhorn Express Pipeline ramp-up. Excluding hedges, this pricing uplift contributed approximately $220 million to our EBITDA growth, or about 40% of the total YoY delta. Notably, our international portfolio shone here: offshore Brazil realizations exceeded $85/bbl on Buzios Phase 3 ramp-up, while North Sea Brent-linked production saw a 12% premium due to favorable fiscal terms post our recent UK tax relief negotiations.

Second, production volumes grew 7% YoY to a record quarterly average of 285,000 boe/d, adding another $180 million to EBITDA. This was led by our U.S. onshore assets, where Permian output surged 14% to 165,000 boe/d, fueled by the completion of 28 new horizontal wells in the Delaware Basin with average laterals exceeding 12,000 feet and proppant intensity at 2,500 lbs/ft. We've leaned into our multi-well pad drilling strategy, achieving a drilling efficiency of 650 feet per day per rig—up 20% YoY—while our completion crews optimized slickwater fracs with 40/70 mesh sand blends, delivering initial production rates averaging 1,800 boe/d per well. Regionally, Eagle Ford contributed a steady 45,000 boe/d with low-decline Eagle Ford Shale cores, and our Bakken position added 12% growth via two new pads tied into the Dakota Access Pipeline. Internationally, Guyana's Liza Phase 2 offshore ramp-up—partnered with ExxonMobil and Hess—added 18,000 boe/d at low breakeven costs under $35/boe, while Brazil's pre-salt reservoirs maintained 92% uptime despite seasonal monsoons.

Third, operational efficiencies and cost discipline drove a $140 million EBITDA uplift, offsetting inflationary pressures in tubulars and sand, which rose 8% industry-wide per EIA data. Lifting costs—or lease operating expenses—fell 11% to $8.20/boe, our lowest in five years, thanks to our 'Fit-for-Future' program. This included digital twin deployments across 40% of Permian assets, using AI-driven predictive maintenance from Halliburton’s DecisionSpace platform, which reduced unplanned downtime by 25% and extended ESP run lives to 850 days. We also captured $45 million in G&A savings through workforce optimization and shared services consolidation post our $1.2 billion divestiture of non-core Rockies assets to Occidental Petroleum earlier this year. Upstream capex efficiency improved with a 15% reduction in drilling days per well, benchmarking in the first quartile per Enverus analytics.

Offsetting these positives modestly were higher royalties in high-price environments—up 5% to 18.5% of revenues—and weather-related disruptions in the North Sea, where Storm Babet curtailed 5,000 boe/d for two weeks. However, our hedging program mitigated 60% of our oil volumes at a $75/bbl floor, providing stability.

Strategically, this EBITDA growth reinforces our capital allocation framework: 50% to shareholder returns via our $0.75/share dividend and $1.5 billion buyback authorization, 40% to organic growth in Tier 1 acreage like Permian and Guyana, and 10% to energy transition initiatives such as our 500,000 tonne/year CCUS hub in the Permian, which qualified for 45Q tax credits and positions us for blue hydrogen offtake with Chevron.

Before we open it up to questions, I'd like to spend a few minutes on our capital allocation framework, which remains the cornerstone of our shareholder value creation strategy here at Apex. As you know, we've generated robust free cash flow of $1.8 billion in Q3 alone—up 25% year-over-year—driven by our Permian Basin outperformance and steady realizations from our LNG cargoes into Europe and Asia. For the full year, we're now guiding to $6.2 billion in FCF at our base case of $75 WTI and $3.50 Henry Hub, even after absorbing the recent OPEC+ production cuts and softer Urals differentials out of the North Sea.

Our capital allocation priorities are clear and disciplined: first, sustainable dividends to reward our loyal shareholders; second, opportunistic share buybacks to accretively enhance per-share metrics; and third, targeted reinvestment in high-return, resilient projects that extend our inventory life beyond 15 years. This 'returns first, growth second' approach has delivered a total shareholder return of 28% YTD, outpacing both the XLE and our supermajor peers like ExxonMobil and Chevron.

Dividends remain our top priority, representing about 40% of our annual FCF, or roughly $2.5 billion this year. We're proud to have increased our base quarterly dividend by 8% to $0.65 per share earlier this year—our 17th consecutive annual hike—yielding a forward 3.8% at current prices, which sits comfortably in the sweet spot between ConocoPhillips' 3.2% and Occidental's more aggressive 4.5%. Our payout ratio stands at a prudent 35% of adjusted earnings, giving us ample dry powder even in a $60 oil downside case. Looking ahead, we've got a progressive dividend policy tied to our long-term FCF generation. With our debt-to-capital ratio now at 18%—down from 25% at the start of the cycle—and net debt at just 0.8x EBITDAX, we're well-positioned to sustain or grow this through the decade. Regional dynamics play in here too: our Middle East JV dividends from the ADNOC-partnered sour gas projects in the UAE are flowing steadily at $400 million annually, hedging us against pure upstream volatility.

Next, share repurchases, which we've allocated 25% of FCF toward, or $1.55 billion YTD. We completed 75% of our $2 billion authorization in Q3, retiring 4.2% of shares outstanding at an average price of $112—well below our intrinsic NAV per share of $145, based on discounted cash flow models incorporating $70 long-term oil. This drove a 12% EPS accretion in the quarter, mirroring what we've seen from peers like Pioneer Natural Resources pre-merger. Our buyback cadence is opportunistic and framework-driven: we pause below $65 WTI but accelerate above $80, with 60% executed via 10b5-1 plans to minimize market timing risk. We've avoided the trap of buying into overvalued peaks, unlike some E&Ps that repurchased at $130+ in 2022. Post-buyback, our float is leaner, boosting EPS growth to 15-18% in 2025 even at flat production.

Finally, reinvestment at 35% of FCF, or $2.2 billion this year, focused on projects delivering IRRs north of 20% at $60 oil. We're not chasing volume for volume's sake—our capex efficiency has improved 30% since 2021 through longer laterals, enhanced completions with 4,000-pound proppant per foot, and AI-optimized frac designs in the Permian, where our Delaware Basin half-cycle payback is now under 7 months. Key initiatives include: Permian Core: $1.1 billion into 120 new Wolfcamp and Bone Springs wells, targeting 10% oil cuts and 1,200 BTU-rich gas. We've secured 50,000 acres of Tier 1 acreage via bolt-ons, mirroring EOG Resources' model, with Q3 IP rates averaging 2,400 boe/d—15% above type curve. International Upside: $600 million into Guyana offshore, where our Stabroek block partner Exxon approved the Yellowtail Phase 2 FPSO, adding 200,000 bbl/d by 2026 at sub-$40 breakevens. In Brazil's pre-salt Santos Basin, we're progressing our Buzios JV with Petrobras, with first oil from our cluster in H2 2025. Energy Transition Plays: $300 million into CCUS and low-carbon ventures, including our $500 million partnership with Occidental for direct air capture in the Permian and a blue hydrogen offtake with Linde for our Freeport LNG trains. This isn't greenwashing—it's capturing 45Q credits and positioning for EU CBAM tariffs, with blended returns still at 18% IRR.

Regionally, we're tilting toward the U.S. Lower 48 (65% of capex) for its resilience amid global LNG oversupply risks from Qatar and U.S. Gulf Coast builds, while de-risking offshore exposure post-Hurricane season. Strategically, this framework flexes with the cycle: in surplus cash years like this, we return 65%+ to shareholders; in downturns, we pivot to inventory. Our ROIC target remains 12-15%, above our 8% WACC, ensuring we're not just returning capital but compounding it. Compared to supermajors, our upstream purity gives us higher FCF yields—12% versus Chevron's 9%—while our inventory depth rivals Diamondback Energy's. We're committed to this discipline, and I hope that gives you confidence in our path to $25 billion cumulative FCF through 2028.

Today, I'd like to dive into our operating expenses per barrel of oil equivalent—or OpEx per BOE—which continues to be a cornerstone of our value creation story at Apex Energy. As you know, in the upstream Oil & Gas sector, managing OpEx per BOE is critical for sustaining free cash flow generation, especially in a volatile WTI environment hovering around $75 to $80 per barrel and Henry Hub gas prices in the $2.50 to $3.00 range. For Q3, our total cash operating expenses per BOE came in at $11.25, a 7% sequential improvement from $12.10 in Q2 and a robust 18% year-over-year decline from $13.75 in Q3 2023. This marks our lowest quarterly OpEx per BOE since we ramped up our Permian position in 2021. On a trailing 12-month basis, we're now at $11.80 per BOE, putting us in the top quartile of peers like Pioneer Natural Resources and EOG Resources, based on recent Enverus benchmarking data.

To give you a clear trend analysis, let's look at the progression over the past eight quarters: From Q4 2022 at $14.50 per BOE amid post-COVID inflation peak, down to Q1 2023 at $14.20 with supply chain normalization, Q2 2023 at $13.90 from initial Permian synergies, Q3 2023 at $13.75 thanks to water recycling rollout, Q4 2023 at $13.20 with automation pilots, Q1 2024 at $12.80 from drilling efficiency gains, Q2 2024 at $12.10 via hedged service contracts, and now Q3 2024 at $11.25 with full digital integration. This downward trajectory reflects not just scale from our production growing 15% YoY to 250,000 BOE/d, but deliberate cost management amid persistent inflationary pressures in tubular goods—up 8% industry-wide per EIA data—and labor costs in high-demand basins.

Breaking it down by component, lease operating expenses—or LOE—accounted for 55% of our total at $6.20 per BOE, down 12% YoY, driven by optimized workover programs. Gathering, processing, and transportation—or GPT—came in at $3.45 per BOE, a 10% reduction thanks to our midstream JV with Enterprise Products Partners. Production taxes ticked up slightly to $1.60 per BOE due to higher realizations in the Permian at 95% of WTI, but this was more than offset elsewhere. Regionally, our performance varies as expected. In the Permian Delaware Basin, where 65% of our production sits, OpEx per BOE is a market-leading $9.80—down 22% YoY—benefiting from pad drilling efficiencies and our proprietary hydraulic fracturing designs using lower proppant intensity, averaging 1,800 pounds per foot. Contrast that with our Eagle Ford assets at $13.50 per BOE, where wet gas economics and higher compression costs persist, but we've clawed back 15% through electrification of artificial lift systems, reducing diesel consumption by 25%. Offshore Gulf of Mexico, representing 10% of output, remains our highest at $18.20 per BOE due to subsea integrity work and hurricane-related deferrals, but we're on track to shave 10% off that in 2025 via ROV drone inspections.

Now, turning to our cost management strategies—these aren't one-offs; they're embedded in our operating DNA. First, technological initiatives: We've fully deployed our 'Apex Digital Field' platform across 80% of our Permian acreage, leveraging AI-driven predictive maintenance from Halliburton’s DecisionSpace and real-time IoT sensors. This has cut unplanned downtime by 30%, directly lowering LOE by optimizing ESP run lives from 18 to 24 months. We're also piloting drone-based leak detection, reducing methane emissions compliance costs by 15% ahead of EPA mandates. Second, supply chain resilience: Facing steel price volatility—up 12% in Q3 per SteelBenchmarker—we locked in 70% of our 2025 tubular and frac sand needs via multi-year contracts with Tenaris and Hi-Crush, hedging against tariffs and Red Sea disruptions. This secured us at $450 per ton for sand, 20% below spot.

Third, water and environmental stewardship: In water-scarce Permian, our recycled water utilization hit 85% in Q3, up from 60% last year, via our produced water swaps with Occidental and partnerships with WaterBridge. This slashed freshwater trucking costs by $1.20 per BOE equivalent. Fourth, portfolio optimization: We're high-grading via divestitures—closing the $450 million sale of non-core DJ Basin assets next quarter—and reallocating capital to sub-$10/BOE half-cycle return inventory. This includes extending laterals to 12,000 feet in the Delaware with enhanced completions using dissolvable diverting agents from Liberty Oilfield Services.

Strategically, these efforts align with our goal of sub-$10 per BOE OpEx by 2026, supporting 20%+ returns at $60 WTI. We're guiding Q4 at $11.00 to $11.50 per BOE, assuming no major service cost inflation, with full-year 2024 at $11.70. Headwinds like potential RIN credits volatility under the Biden renewable mandates are in our models, but our hedging—65% of 2025 service costs capped—mitigates upside risk. In summary, our OpEx discipline underscores Apex's competitive moat, delivering peer-beating cash margins of 45% in Q3. We're not just cutting costs; we're engineering sustainable efficiencies for the energy transition.

I'll now turn to our operational efficiency metrics, specifically lifting costs per BOE, where we've made meaningful progress amid a challenging macro environment. As you know, lifting costs—or lease operating expenses (LOE)—represent the cash costs to produce and maintain our producing assets, excluding G&A, taxes, and upstream capex. We report this on a BOE basis to normalize across our diverse portfolio of conventional and unconventional assets.

Let me start with the trend analysis. Over the past five years, our company-wide lifting costs have followed a classic Oil & Gas lifecycle pattern, influenced by the post-pandemic recovery, supply chain disruptions, and inflationary pressures on labor and materials. Back in Q2 2020, during the depths of the WTI crash, our LOE averaged $12.45 per BOE, reflecting deferred maintenance and curtailed ops to preserve cash. By Q4 2022, amid surging energy demand and OPEC+ cuts, costs had climbed to a peak of $18.75 per BOE—a 50% YoY increase—driven by 25% inflation in tubular goods, chemicals, and third-party services, plus higher workover activity to restore sidelined wells.

Fast-forward to Q3 2024, and we're thrilled to report a sequential decline to $14.20 per BOE, down 8% from Q1's $15.45 and 12% below the 2023 average of $16.10. This marks our lowest quarterly LOE since Q3 2021, ahead of our full-year guidance midpoint of $14.50–$15.00. Year-to-date, we've shaved $1.85 per BOE off last year's run-rate, directly contributing $185 million to EBITDAX on our 110 MMBOE production base. Excluding one-offs like the $25 million weather-related repairs in the Gulf of Mexico from Q1, the underlying trend is even stronger at $13.90 per BOE.

Breaking it down regionally, our U.S. onshore assets continue to anchor efficiency. In the Permian Basin—our core growth engine, now 55% of production—LOE fell to $9.80 per BOE in Q3, down from $11.20 in Q1 and crushing the basin benchmark of $12–$14 as reported by EIA and peers like Pioneer and Occidental. This reflects mature field optimizations in the Delaware sub-basin, where we've optimized artificial lift conversions from rod pumps to ESPs on 15% of our 2,500-well inventory. Eagle Ford held steady at $10.50 per BOE, benefiting from shared services with our Midland ops. Internationally, challenges persist but are improving. North Sea assets averaged $22.40 per BOE, down 6% QoQ, thanks to platform debottlenecking at our Buzzard field analogue—modeled after Sullom Voe efficiencies seen at EnQuest. Gulf of Mexico shelf and deepwater came in at $28.75 per BOE, elevated due to subsea integrity work on our Holstein-style tie-backs, but we've clawed back to pre-Ursula storm levels through ROV-deployed inspections reducing diving costs by 30%.

Now, turning to our cost reduction initiatives—these aren't one-offs; they're embedded in our 'Efficiency 2.0' program, targeting $2.00–$3.00 per BOE savings by year-end 2025. First, digital transformation: We've rolled out AspenTech's HYSYS digital twins across 70% of our Permian facilities, enabling predictive maintenance that cut unplanned downtime by 22% QoQ. AI-driven anomaly detection on our SCADA systems flagged 450 pump failures pre-emptively, saving $0.45 per BOE in workover rig time alone—similar to Chevron's Hammerhead AI playbook. Second, water and chemical optimization: Produced water handling is 25% of LOE in shale plays. We've partnered with SLB for their Delfzijl electrocoagulation tech, recycling 85% of water volumes in the Permian—up from 65% last year—slashing disposal costs from $1.20 to $0.75 per BOE. Our in-house chemical program, using bio-based corrosion inhibitors akin to Nalco Champion's offerings, reduced treating expenses by 18%, or $0.60 per BOE.

Third, supply chain and contracting: Post-2022 inflation, we locked in 3-year master service agreements with Halliburton and Baker Hughes at 15% below spot rates, hedging 80% of our tubular and frac sand needs. Regional hubs in Midland and Corpus Christi have centralized inventory, cutting logistics by 12%. In the North Sea, we're emulating Equinor's vendor consolidation, merging contracts to drive 10% savings on helicopter and vessel days. Strategically, these initiatives position us for sustained free cash flow generation even at $60 WTI. Every $1 per BOE reduction lifts our Permian breakevens to under $25 half-cycle—best-in-class versus E&P peers. Post our $1.2 billion Bolt-On acquisition in the Midland Basin, we're realizing $0.75 per BOE synergies through scale, with full run-rate by Q4. Looking ahead, Q4 guidance is $13.80–$14.20 per BOE, assuming stable Brent at $80 and no major hurricanes. We're on track for 10–15% LOE deflation in 2025 as ESP run-life extends to 900 days from 650, and our carbon capture pilots reduce flaring-related fines. In summary, our lifting cost trajectory underscores disciplined execution in a volatile market. This efficiency not only bolsters margins but de-risks our $5–7 billion M&A war chest for bolt-ons in Tier 1 acreage.

Before we open the floor to questions, I'd like to walk you through our capital expenditure performance, focusing on the breakdown across Drilling, Completion, and Facilities. As a reminder, our full-year 2024 capex guidance remains at $4.8 to $5.2 billion, weighted 75% towards the back half of the year to align with our peak drilling and completion cadence in the Permian and Eagle Ford. We continue to prioritize high-return inventory in the core of the Delaware Basin and the oil window of the Eagle Ford, where we've seen IRR uplift from our technical initiatives exceeding 50% on new wells.

Overall, Q3 capex totaled $1.1 billion, coming in 8% under our $1.2 billion quarterly budget—or about $100 million below plan. This underrun was driven by a combination of operational efficiencies, favorable supply chain dynamics, and some weather-related deferrals in facilities work, partially offset by targeted investments in completion innovation.

Drilling: Budget $500 million vs. Actual $480 million (4% underrun). Drilling spend represented 44% of our Q3 total capex, flat sequentially but up from 40% in Q3 2023 as we ramped pads in the Permian. We drilled 52 wells against a budget of 55, primarily due to one rig delay from a BOP recertification on our Patterson-UTI Super Spec 2000 rigs in the Delaware Basin—nothing material, just routine MS-121 compliance. Actual costs per lateral foot came in at $720, a 6% improvement over budget and 12% below Q3 2023, thanks to our rollout of Schlumberger's Stiletto PDC bits optimized for the Wolfcamp A and Second Bone Spring intervals. These bits extended run lengths to 8,500 feet on average, reducing trips by 15%. Regionally, Permian drilling absorbed 70% of this bucket at $336 million (under budget by $14 million), with strong execution on our 10-mile laterals in Lea County, New Mexico. Eagle Ford contributed $120 million, where we're testing GeoSteering 2.0 with Halliburton's DecisionSpace for real-time geosteering, shaving 10-15% off directional costs. Offshore GoM was lighter at $24 million, focused on sidetracks in our Lobster field tie-back. Key trend: Our drilling efficiency metric—lateral feet per rig day—hit 1,200 feet, up 18% YoY, putting us in the top quartile per Enverus analytics. This supports our multi-well pad strategy, where we're stacking 48-well pads to minimize surface footprint and comply with New Mexico's spacing rules.

Completion: Budget $450 million vs. Actual $420 million (7% underrun). Completion, at 38% of Q3 capex, saw the strongest outperformance, driven by frack crew efficiencies and proppant pricing tailwinds. WTI held steady around $82 per barrel through quarter-end, supporting our activity without pressure, while Henry Hub gas at $2.70/MMBtu kept associated gas economics solid. We completed 48 wells vs. 50 budgeted, with costs per stage averaging $45,000—8% under plan. This reflects our shift to dissolvable diverter tech from Liberty Oilfield Services, which enabled zipper fracs across 4-well pads in the Permian, boosting stages per day from 22 to 28. Proppant intensity remains at 2,500 lbs/ft in the core Delaware, using 100-mesh Eagle Ford sand blends to optimize conductivity in our hybrid slickwater designs. Breakout: Permian took $300 million (67% of category), under by $25 million due to accelerated turn-in-lines (TILs) from Q2 inventory—our D&C cycle time is now 45 days, rivaling pioneers like EOG Resources. Eagle Ford $90 million focused on Austin Chalk extensions, where we've reduced cluster spacing to 25 feet with fiber-optic diagnostics, yielding 15% EUR uplift per our PTTC models. GoM completions were $30 million, emphasizing deepwater frac plugs for our Thunder Horse analog. Strategically, we're leaning into electrification: 40% of Q3 frack fleets were electric or hybrid, cutting diesel use by 30% and aligning with our Scope 1 emissions reduction target of 25% by 2025. This also insulated us from fuel volatility amid Red Sea disruptions.

Facilities: Budget $250 million vs. Actual $200 million (20% underrun). Facilities rounded out at 18% of capex, the most deferred bucket at $50 million under budget. This includes midstream tie-ins, water infrastructure, and electrification projects. Deferrals stemmed from wet weather in the Permian delaying SWD well tie-ins and a strategic pause on a $20 million gas plant expansion in Karnes County pending natgas price recovery. Actuals: Permian facilities $140 million, covering centralized produced water recycling at our Eunice hub—now handling 1.2 MMbbl/month with 95% recycle rate, per our produced water agreements with WaterBridge. This dropped our freshwater intensity to 4 bbl/BOE, top-decile vs. Permian peers. Eagle Ford $40 million went to NGL splitter upgrades at our La Salle plant, capturing more Y-grade for export amid Mont Belvieu frac spreads widening to $0.25/gal. GoM $20 million for subsea manifolds on Lobster. Trend insight: Facilities capex per BOE is down 22% YoY to $3.50, thanks to modular prefab units pioneered by companies like Chart Industries, slashing install time by 40%. We're also advancing our CO2 flood pilot in the Permian, with $15 million invested in vapor recovery units to support EOR scalability.

In aggregate, these efficiencies generated $100 million in free cash flow uplift, reinforcing our Q3 levered FCF of $450 million at strip prices. Drilling & Completions (D&C) as 82% of total capex underscores our development focus, with facilities scaling back to high-ROI items only. Compared to peers like Pioneer and Occidental, our capex intensity is 10% lower at $8.50/BOE, driven by 20/20/20 tech suite: 20% longer laterals, 20% fewer clusters, 20% less water. Looking forward, Q4 capex will ramp to $1.4 billion, with Drilling +5% QoQ on rig adds, Completion flat, and Facilities +15% for winterized infrastructure. Risks include rig rate inflation (currently $28k/day) and steel tariffs, but our frame agreements with NOV and Weatherford mitigate that. We're well-positioned for Brent at $85+ to accelerate share repurchases.

I'll turn the call over to David Rodriguez for an operational update.

David Rodriguez: Thank you, Sarah. On the operational front, we continue to execute our strategy effectively. Our production averaged 280,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. We successfully brought Blackhawk Cube wells online, which are expected to contribute significantly to our production growth in the coming quarters. We are also making progress on our cost reduction initiatives.

Now I will turn it over to Steve Harlan for an update on our exploration activities.

Steve Harlan: Thank you, David. Good afternoon, everyone. Today, I'll dive into our exploration and drilling updates, highlighting key well results from the quarter and our forward plans. We've continued to execute with discipline in a volatile macro environment, with WTI averaging $78 per barrel and Henry Hub natural gas holding steady around $2.80 per MMBtu. Our focus remains on high-return inventory in Tier 1 acreage, leveraging advanced completion designs to drive capital efficiency.

Starting with the big picture: In Q3, we spudded 28 wells across our core basins, brought online 32 wells, and maintained an average of 12 active drilling rigs—up from 10 in Q2. Our drilling efficiency continues to improve, with average days to drill now at 18 days per well, a 12% reduction year-over-year, thanks to optimized pad drilling and our partnership with Halliburton on high-performance drill bits. Completion costs per lateral foot fell 8% sequentially to $950, driven by our shift to 40-stage fracs with 3,500 pounds per foot proppant intensity using our proprietary ceramic blends.

Let me break this down by region, starting with the Permian Basin, which accounted for 65% of our drilling capex this quarter. Our Permian program delivered exceptional results. We brought online the inaugural six wells from our "Blackhawk Cube" development in Loving County, Texas—our first true cube-style project with 12,000-foot laterals stacked across Wolfcamp A, B, and C benches. These wells posted an average IP30 of 1,450 boe/d (75% oil), smashing our type curve by 18% and outperforming peers like Pioneer Natural Resources' recent Solomon Field disclosures. Estimated ultimate recovery (EUR) per well is tracking at 1.4 million boe, based on our proprietary decline curve analytics and pressure transient analysis from our petrophysical team. Notably, Well #BH-41L achieved a peak IP of 2,100 boe/d, our strongest Permian result to date, thanks to our engineered completion using dissolvable diverters and 25% more sand than our 2023 baseline. Child well interference was minimal at under 5% production degradation, validated by our fiber-optic DTS monitoring. Overall Permian success rate was 99%, with drilling costs averaging $8.2 million per well—down 15% from Q3 last year. We're seeing a clear trend: well productivity up 22% YoY on a lateral-foot basis, fueled by our multi-bench targeting and simultaneous frac operations (SIMOPS), which reduced cycle times by 25%. Regionally, our 85,000 net acres in the Delaware core remain Tier 1, with over 3,500 locations at $40/bbl half-cycle returns. Midland contributions were solid too, with four wells in Martin County IP'ing at 1,100 boe/d average, aligning with EOG Resources' South Texas-type performance.

Shifting south, our Eagle Ford assets—centered in Karnes and DeWitt Counties—continue to be a cash flow machine. We online'd eight wells, averaging IP30 of 950 boe/d (55% oil, 35% NGLs), with EURs of 850,000 boe. Standout was the "Rattlesnake 7H" well, which hit 1,400 boe/d IP30 after a 10,000-foot lateral with our optimized slickwater frac design incorporating 2,500 psi closure stress beads from Liberty Oilfield Services. Costs here dropped to $6.5 million per well, a 10% sequential improvement, despite some service inflation. Production efficiency is up 15% YoY, and we're capitalizing on strong Gulf Coast NGL pricing—our realized NGL price was $28/bbl in Q3. We've de-risked 400 locations here, with IRRs exceeding 60% at current strips.

In the Bakken, we spudded four extended laterals in our McKenzie County block. The three online wells averaged IP30 of 1,200 boe/d (85% oil), with EURs of 1.1 million boe—10% above our internal type curve. Well #MB-22X featured a 14,500-foot lateral across the Middle Bakken, using our geo-steering tech with Schlumberger's Drillbit DPS system to stay in the sweet spot. Costs held at $9.8 million per well, competitive with Continental Resources' benchmarks. Challenges included minor weather delays, but our rig utilization was 95%. This basin provides diversification, with low breakevens around $45/bbl WTI.

On the exploration front, we achieved a milestone with the "Gulfstar-1" appraisal well on our Walker Ridge block offshore Louisiana. This high-impact test flowed 5,200 boe/d on a 64/64 choke during early flowback, confirming 150 feet of net pay in Miocene sands. We're estimating 50-75 MMboe EUR for the structure, with a sub-$30/bbl breakeven. Partners include Chevron, and we're fast-tracking a subsea tie-back to existing infrastructure, targeting first oil in H2 2026. In Appalachia, our Utica dry gas program spudded two pilots in Ohio, posting IP90 rates of 25 MMcf/d per well. With natgas prices firming, these 12,000-foot laterals offer quick payouts at under 18 months.

Looking ahead, our 2025 drilling plan calls for 140-160 wells, with capex of $1.2-1.3 billion allocated 70% to Permian, 20% Eagle Ford, and 10% Bakken/exploration. We'll run 14 rigs on average, ramping to 16 in Q1 on Permian pads. DDP inventory stands at 4,200 locations (10+ years at current pace), all with half-cycle returns >50% at $60 WTI. Key initiatives include: Tech Ramp: Rolling out AI-driven frac optimization with Baker Hughes' JewelSuite, targeting 10-15% uplift in EURs. Efficiency: Full adoption of walked-up SIMOPS across 80% of pads, shaving 20-30 days off cycles. Sustainability: 100% electrified fracs in new Permian developments, cutting Scope 1 emissions 25%. We're also progressing our CCUS pilot in the Permian with Occidental's STRATOS project. Hedging Discipline: 55% of 2025 oil hedged at $72/bbl floor. We're positioned for multi-year growth amid OPEC+ cuts and LNG export ramps supporting natgas. Risks include service costs and regulatory hurdles, but our inventory quality and operational moat give us conviction. We are excited about the potential of our exploration program. We recently completed a successful seismic survey in Permian Basin and are planning to drill 28 exploration wells in the next year. We believe these wells have the potential to add significant reserves to our portfolio.

Finally, I'll turn it over to Lisa Chen to discuss our marketing strategy.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Steve. We are focused on optimizing our marketing strategy to maximize the value of our production. We are seeing strong demand for renewable diesel in Gulf Coast, and we are working to expand our customer base and strengthen our relationships with existing customers. The impact of this product is significant, contributing about 45% of our adjusted EBITDA this quarter, up from 38% a year ago. Overall, it was a solid quarter with throughput ahead of expectations, margins holding resilient despite softer diesel cracks, and efficiency gains from our recent turnaround optimizations. We averaged 1.45 million barrels per day across our five U.S. refineries—Gulf Coast, Midwest PADD 2, and West Coast assets—for a utilization rate of 94%, up 300 basis points sequentially and 5% year-over-year. This compares favorably to the peer group average of 89%, per EIA data. Our flagship 350 Mbpd Gulf Coast complex in Port Arthur ran at 98% utilization post its Q2 partial turnaround, processing a diverse slate with 65% sour crudes from Latin America and the Middle East, leveraging our high Nelson Complexity Index of 12.5. Midwest throughput hit 420 Mbpd, benefiting from strong regional demand for Group II base oils and ULSD. On the West Coast, our 280 Mbpd Martinez facility operated at 92%, navigating California’s Low Carbon Fuel Standard headwinds but capturing premium jet fuel cracks amid summer travel peaks. Seasonally adjusted, this puts us on track for full-year throughput of 1.42 MMbpd, a 4% improvement YoY, driven by lighter maintenance schedules—we only had 25 days of planned downtime versus 45 days last year. Looking ahead, Q4 utilization should tick up to 95-96%, assuming no hurricane disruptions in the USGC.

Our realized refining margin was $18.50 per barrel on a 3:2:1 crack basis, down 12% sequentially from $21.10 but still 15% above the five-year average. This reflects the diesel crack compression we all saw—Group III ULSD fell to $25/bbl in the USGC from $35/bbl in Q2, pressured by inverted WTI-Brent spreads and high European refinery runs post-Russian sanctions. Gasoline held up better at $22/bbl 3:2:1, supported by driving season demand and E10 blend economics. Regionally, Gulf Coast margins shone at $20.20/bbl, capturing $4/bbl export premia to Latin America and Asia, where our hydrocracker yields 55% middle distillates. Midwest margins were $16.80/bbl, buoyed by $2.50/bbl premia on renewable diesel co-processing—we hit 15,000 bpd of HRD production, qualifying for D4 RINs at $1.80 each. West Coast was softer at $14.50/bbl due to $8/bbl ARB credits offset by elevated CARB diesel specs, but our pre-treatment units kept compliance costs flat QoQ. Product slate optimization was key: middle distillate yields rose to 52% from 49% YoY via better VGO routing, while gasoline octane barrels benefited from our alkylation expansions. Inventory FIFO impacts added $0.80/bbl tailwind this quarter. Full-year margin guidance holds at $17.50-$19.50/bbl, with upside if Brent stays above $75 and diesel rebounds on winter heating demand.

Operational efficiency—this is where we're pulling ahead. Cash operating costs per barrel fell to $6.10, down 8% YoY and 3% sequentially, beating our $6.50 target. Key drivers: energy intensity dropped 5% to 85,000 BTU per barrel through our $150 million digital twin initiative at Port Arthur, which optimizes crude distillation tower operations using AI predictive analytics—similar to what Valero's implemented successfully. We also commissioned a new $80 million coker revamp in the Midwest, boosting residue conversion by 10% and cutting fuel oil production to under 2% of output. Turnaround efficiency was stellar: the Port Arthur event came in 15% under budget at $220 million, with hydrotreater catalyst loadings using next-gen Chevron zeolite tech extending run lengths to 5 years. Maintenance CapEx was $450 million this quarter, on pace for $1.8 billion full-year. Yield capture improved to 102.5% of theoretical, thanks to our proprietary asphaltene solver model reducing fouling in the vacuum unit. Strategically, we're leaning into energy transition plays: 20% of Gulf Coast throughput now includes renewable feedstocks, targeting 50,000 bpd HRD by 2025 with pre-treated waste oils, positioning us like Marathon's San Diego pivot. We're also exporting 250 Mbpd of products, hedging 60% of Q4 cracks via NYMEX futures to lock in $18+ floors. Amid IMO 2020 sulfur cap compliance, our scrubber retrofits on marine fuel units are yielding $3/bbl premia. In summary, refining delivered $1.2 billion in segment EBITDA, up 22% YoY, with ROIC at 18%. We're well-positioned for volatility, focusing on high-complexity runs, cost discipline, and sustainable fuels.
